What Should a Marathon Training Plan Include?

A good marathon training plan includes seven things: enough weeks to build safely, a long run that grows gradually, mostly easy running with a little hard work, mileage that rises slowly, regular cutback weeks, a two- to three-week taper, and practice with race-day fueling. This page explains what each element should look like, so you can judge any plan. It then helps you choose one of our complete week-by-week schedules.

Already know what you need? Jump to the plan comparison table.

What a good marathon training plan includes

1. Enough weeks for your starting point

Most marathon plans run 16–20 weeks. The right length depends on your current mileage, not your ambition. Runners already covering 25–30 miles (40–48 km) a week can be ready in 16 weeks. A base of 10–15 miles a week needs closer to six months. Very short plans of 12 weeks or less only work for runners who are already fit for long distances.

2. A long run that builds gradually

The weekly long run is the core of marathon training. A good plan raises it by about 1–2 miles (2–3 km) a week, steps it back every third or fourth week, and peaks at 18–22 miles (29–35 km), or about 3–3.5 hours, whichever comes first. Schedule the longest run 3–5 weeks before race day. You don't need to run 26.2 miles in training: the long run, the weeks of consistent volume behind it, and the taper together prepare you for the full distance.

3. Mostly easy running, a little hard

Roughly 80% of your running should be at an easy, conversational pace, and about 20% should be harder: threshold runs, intervals and marathon-pace work. Easy days have to be truly easy, so that the hard sessions can be hard. A plan that makes every run "moderate" is a red flag.

  • First marathon: one short workout a week is enough, often just strides or a few minutes at threshold.
  • Experienced runners: one workout plus one marathon-pace run, or a long run that finishes at marathon pace.

4. Mileage that rises slowly

Look for weekly increases of about 10%, and never much more than 15%. Big jumps in volume are a common cause of running injuries such as shin pain and stress reactions. How high the plan peaks depends on your experience:

  • First-time marathoners: 30–40 miles (48–64 km) a week is plenty.
  • Runners chasing a time: typically 45–60 miles (72–97 km).

5. Cutback weeks

Every third or fourth week should drop by about 20–25%. Your body absorbs training during these weeks, and they make it far more likely that you reach the start line healthy.

6. A two- to three-week taper

Volume falls over the final 2–3 weeks: to roughly 75–85% of your peak, then 60–70%, and then a light race week. Keep some short, faster running so your legs stay sharp. A taper longer than three weeks starts to cost fitness. One shorter than two leaves you tired on race day.

7. Fueling practice

Your gut can be trained like your legs. On long runs over about 90 minutes, take 30–60 g of carbohydrate per hour, using the same gels or drinks you will race with. Some runners build up to more. For the 36–48 hours before the race, eat a high-carbohydrate diet, roughly 8–10 g per kg of body weight per day, and cut back on fibre. Drink to thirst, and use electrolytes in hot weather.

8. Strength training and rest days

Two short strength sessions a week reduce injury risk and help you hold your form late in the race. Good exercises include squats, lunges, step-ups, calf raises and core work. Drop to one session in the taper. Every plan should also include at least one full rest day a week. Sleep is part of training.

How to choose a marathon training plan

Answer four questions, then pick the matching row in the table below:

  1. How many weeks until race day?
  2. What do you run now? Use your average weekly mileage over the last month. Start a plan whose week 1 is close to that figure.
  3. How many days a week can you run? Three or four is enough for a first marathon. Five or six suits faster goals.
  4. What's your goal? Finishing, a time target, or a personal best?

Red flags in a marathon plan

  • Weekly mileage that jumps by 20% or more, or has no cutback weeks.
  • A long run of more than 22 miles (35 km), or more than about 3.5 hours, for non-elite runners.
  • Hard sessions on back-to-back days, every week.
  • A taper of less than two weeks, or more than three.
  • A starting week far above what you run now.

FAQ

Can you train for a marathon in 1 month?

Only if you are already close to marathon fitness, for example if you recently ran a half marathon and regularly run 25+ miles a week with long runs of 13+ miles. Starting from little running, one month isn't enough to prepare your muscles, tendons and bones, and the risk of injury is high. Pick a race 4–6 months out, or run a 10K or half marathon first.

How long should a marathon training plan be?

Usually 16–20 weeks. Choose 24 weeks if your current base is under about 15 miles a week. Choose 12–16 weeks only if you already run 30+ miles a week.

How many days a week should I run when training for a marathon?

Three to four days works for many first-timers. Runners aiming for faster times typically run five or six. More days only help if the extra runs are easy.

Do you need to run 20 miles before a marathon?

Not exactly 20 miles, but most runners benefit from a peak long run of 18–22 miles (29–35 km), or about 3–3.5 hours, whichever comes first, done 3–5 weeks before the race.
keyTakeaway: A good marathon plan matches your current mileage, builds the long run and weekly volume gradually with cutback weeks, keeps most running easy, and ends with a 2-3 week taper.
